column3: Team Norms
column5:
As a team, create a parent page in Confluence called "Team Norms". This page will contain the following child pages:

* Working Agreement
* Definition of Ready
* Definition of Done
* GitFlow
column6:
* A parent page titled "Team Norms" exists in Confluence
* The "Team Norms" page has four child pages created with the following exact titles:
** Working Agreement
** Definition of Ready
** Definition of Done
** GitFlow
* All four child pages are properly linked/nested under the "Team Norms" parent page
* The parent-child page hierarchy is visible in Confluence's page navigation
* All pages are accessible to the intended team members

column3: Working Agreement
column5: As a team, create a team Working Agreement that defines how the team will work together and hold each other accountable.
column6:
* A child page titled "Working Agreement" is created under the "Team Norms" parent page in Confluence
* The Working Agreement is documented on the page and accessible to all team members
* All team members participate in creating the agreement
* The agreement includes the following sections:
** Working Hours - Core hours when team members are available and agreed meeting times
** Communication - How to communicate absences and unavailability
** Team Collaboration - Guidelines for respectful communication and ensuring all voices are heard
** Scrum Practices - Team-specific agile practices (e.g., when to escalate blockers, keeping Jira updated)
** Version Control - Git workflow rules (e.g., no direct commits to main, PR review timeframes)
* All team members commit to following the agreement
* A process for handling disagreements during creation is documented

Note: Keep the agreement concise and focused on the most important team norms.

column3: Definition of Done
column5: As a team, create a Definition of Done that establishes clear criteria for when features, sprints, and releases are production-ready.
column6:
* A child page titled "Definition of Done" is created under the "Team Norms" parent page in Confluence
* The Definition of Done includes all three sections with at least 3 criteria each:
** Feature/User Story Done:
*** All acceptance criteria met
*** Unit tests written and passing
*** Code reviewed and approved
*** No critical bugs or blockers
** Sprint Done:
*** All committed stories completed
*** Code merged to appropriate branch
*** All tests passing (unit, integration)
*** Sprint demo completed
** Release Done:
*** All sprint DoD criteria met
*** Security scan completed
*** Documentation updated
*** Responsive design verified
*** Ready for production deployment
* All team members participate in creating and approve the final criteria
* A review cadence is established (e.g., during retrospectives)

*Success Metrics:*

* Minimum 3 criteria per section
* 100% team participation and documented approval

column3: GitFlow
column5: As a team, establish a GitFlow branching model and CI/CD pipeline strategy for all team code repositories.
column6:
* A child page titled "GitFlow" is created under the "Team Norms" parent page in Confluence
* The GitFlow document defines the branching strategy with CI/CD pipelines for key branch types:
** Main Branch:
*** Triggers: On merge/push
*** Pipeline: Full test suite, security scanning, production deployment (with approval gate), smoke tests
*** Protection: Requires PR approval, no direct commits
** Develop Branch:
*** Triggers: On merge/push
*** Pipeline: Full test suite, code quality checks (linting, ≥80% coverage), deploy to staging
*** Protection: Requires PR approval
** Feature Branches (feature/*):
*** Naming convention defined (e.g., feature/JIRA-123-description)
*** Unit tests written and passing
** Release Branches (release/*):
*** Triggers: On creation/push
*** Pipeline: Full test suite, security audit, deploy to pre-production, QA testing window
*** Version tagging strategy defined
** Hotfix Branches (hotfix/*):
*** Triggers: On creation/push/PR
*** Pipeline: Targeted tests, regression suite, security check, expedited deployment to staging
*** Fast-track review process defined
* Branch protection rules documented for main and develop branches
* Merge strategies specified (squash, rebase, or merge commit)
* All team members participate in creating and approve the workflow

*Success Metrics:*

* Pipelines configured for key branches
* Zero unauthorized deployments to production
* 100% of deployments traceable to source branch

column3: Code Review Standards
column5: As a team, create Code Review Standards that define PR review expectations including turnaround time and what to look for.
column6:
* A child page titled "Code Review Standards" is created under the "Team Norms" parent page in Confluence
* The page is accessible to all team members
* The Code Review Standards include the following sections:
** Review Turnaround Time:
*** Initial review within 24 hours
*** Urgent/hotfix reviews within 4 hours
*** Follow-up reviews within 12 hours
** PR Size Guidelines:
*** Ideal PR size (e.g., <400 lines of code)
*** When to split large PRs
** What to Review:
*** Code correctness and logic
*** Code readability and maintainability
*** Test coverage and quality
*** Security vulnerabilities
*** Performance implications
*** Documentation and comments
*** Adherence to coding standards
** PR Requirements:
*** Descriptive title and description
*** Link to Jira ticket
*** All tests passing
*** No merge conflicts
*** At least one reviewer approval required
** Review Etiquette:
*** Be respectful and constructive
*** Explain the "why" behind comments
*** Distinguish between required changes and suggestions
* All team members participate in creating and approve the standards

column3: Definition of Ready
column5: As a team, create a Definition of Ready that establishes clear criteria for when user stories and sprints are ready to begin.
column6:
* A child page titled "Definition of Ready" is created under the "Team Norms" parent page in Confluence
* The page is accessible to all team members
* The Definition of Ready includes both of the following sections with a minimum of 3 criteria each:
** Definition of Ready for a User Story:
*** Acceptance criteria are clearly defined
*** Story is estimated with story points
*** Story is assigned to a team member
*** Dependencies are identified
*** Technical approach is understood
** Definition of Ready for a Sprint:
*** Sprint backlog is prioritized
*** All user stories meet the Definition of Ready
*** Sprint goal is defined
*** Team capacity is confirmed
*** No blocking dependencies exist
* All team members participate in creating and agree on the criteria
* Team formally approves the Definition of Ready (documented approval/sign-off)
* A review cadence is established (e.g., after each retrospective)

*Success Metrics:*

* Definition of Ready contains at least 3 criteria per section
* 100% team participation in creation
* Documented team approval/consensus

column3: Create the user and role tables

column6:

column3: Create the credential and mfa_enrollment tables
column5: As a Backend Developer, I want credential and mfa_enrollment tables, so that password hashes and second factors are stored apart from user profile data.
column6:
# A migration creates a credential table holding the argon2id hash keyed to a user.
# An mfa_enrollment table stores a per-user TOTP secret and enrolled flag.
# Neither table stores a plaintext password or recovery code.

column3: Hash and store passwords with argon2id
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want passwords hashed with argon2id on registration, so that no credential is ever stored in plaintext.
column6:
# Registration hashes the password with argon2id and stores only the hash in the credential table.
# The work-factor parameters are configurable and documented.
# A test asserts the stored value is a valid argon2id hash, not the plaintext.

column3: Verify password on login
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want login to verify the password against the argon2id hash, so that only valid credentials proceed to the second factor.
column6:
# Login verifies the submitted password against the stored hash.
# A wrong password returns 401 without revealing whether the email exists.
# A correct password advances to the MFA challenge rather than issuing a token directly.

column3: Enroll a user in TOTP MFA
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want users to enroll a TOTP second factor, so that login requires more than a password.
column6:
# An enroll endpoint generates a TOTP secret and returns a provisioning URI.
# Enrollment is confirmed by submitting a valid current code before the factor is activated.
# The secret is stored in mfa_enrollment and the user is marked enrolled.

column3: Challenge and verify the MFA code at login
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want login to require a valid TOTP code, so that a stolen password alone cannot authenticate.
column6:
# After password verification, login requires a second-factor code.
# An invalid or expired code returns 401 and does not issue a token.
# A valid code proceeds to JWT issuance.

column3: Issue access and refresh JWTs with role and tenant claims
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want the service to issue access and refresh JWTs carrying role and tenant, so that every request carries a verified identity.
column6:
# A successful login issues a short-lived access token and a refresh token with a defined issuer.
# The access token carries the user's role and tenant_id claims.
# The refresh token is persisted in a refresh_token table and can be revoked.

column3: Add JWT validation middleware to protected routes
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want JWT validation middleware on protected routes, so that unauthenticated requests are rejected.
column6:
# Middleware validates the access token signature, expiry, and issuer.
# A request without a valid JWT to a protected route returns 401.
# A valid token exposes role and tenant_id to the request context.

column3: Cover auth negative paths and reject SSO callbacks
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want negative-path auth tests including a rejected SSO callback, so that only the supported email+password+MFA flow can authenticate.
column6:
# Tests assert wrong password, missing MFA, and tampered token each return 401.
# A request to a hypothetical SSO/OIDC callback route returns 404 — SSO is out of scope.
# The negative-path suite runs locally and is green.

column3: Validate shared JWTs in a FastAPI dependency
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want a FastAPI dependency that validates the same JWTs the Node service issues, so that the Tax Calculation Engine trusts one identity scheme.
column6:
# The dependency validates JWT signature, expiry, and issuer using the shared key.
# An expired or tampered token is rejected with 401.
# A valid token exposes role and tenant_id to downstream handlers.

column3: Create the append-only audit_entry table
column5: As a Backend Developer, I want an append-only audit_entry table, so that who-did-what-when is recorded immutably per case.
column6:
# A migration creates audit_entry with case_id, actor, action, reason, result (a success/failure enum), and occurred_at, matching the Module 3 audit schema.
# A database rule or trigger blocks UPDATE and DELETE on audit_entry.

column3: Write an audit entry on every stage transition
column5: As a Firm Admin, I want every stage transition written to the audit trail, so that the Plan Cycle is compliance-defensible.
column6:
# Each successful stage transition writes an append-only audit entry of who-did-what-when.
# The audit write commits with the transition in the same transaction.
# A test asserts a transition produces exactly one audit entry.

column3: Wire the role-gated transition endpoint enforcing the permission matrix
column5: As a Security Engineer, I want the stage-transition validator exposed as a role-gated endpoint, so that only authorized roles advance a Tax Plan Cycle and denials are audited.
column6:
# A PATCH /cycles/{id}/transition endpoint invokes the stage-transition validator for the requested move.
# The endpoint enforces the TaxPulse matrix: Review Sign-Off/Send Back and Close & Seal (→ Archived) require Firm Admin; the Advisor (EDIT) may run Data Aggregation → Modeling → Submit for Review and Present to Client.
# An authorized, legal transition advances the stage and writes the stage_transition row; an illegal move returns 422 and an unauthorized role returns 403, neither mutating the cycle.
# A denied attempt writes an append-only audit entry recording the attempting actor and the attempted transition.
# Tests assert allowed versus denied transitions per role plus the 403 and 422 paths.

column3: Redact income and deduction figures in audit output
column5: As a Firm Admin, I want dollar figures redacted in audit output, so that sensitive amounts are not exposed in the trail.
column6:
# Income and deduction dollar figures are redacted when an audit entry is rendered.
# Redaction is applied at read/serialization time, leaving the stored action intact.
# A test asserts a redacted figure never appears in the audit output.

column3: Enforce per-tenant rate limiting
column5: As a Platform Engineer, I want per-tenant rate limiting, so that one firm cannot exhaust shared capacity.
column6:
# Requests exceeding a per-tenant limit return 429 with a Retry-After header.
# Rate-limit counters are isolated per tenant_id in a shared Redis store (rate-limit-redis), and responses carry the standard IETF RateLimit headers (standardHeaders: "draft-8").
# A test asserts one tenant's burst does not throttle another tenant.

column3: Emit cost-accounting headers per request
column5: As a Platform Engineer, I want cost-accounting headers on responses, so that per-request usage is observable.
column6:
# Responses include a header reporting the request's accounted cost units.
# The cost value reflects the operation performed.
# A test asserts the header is present on a representative endpoint.

column5: As a Backend Developer, I want the Plan Cycle API served under a /v1 prefix, so that the Core Case Service can evolve without breaking consumers.
column6:
# All Plan Cycle endpoints are served under a /v1 prefix.

column5: As a Backend Developer, I want an ADR documenting which entity each service owns, so that bounded contexts stay clear as the system grows.
column6:
# An ADR states that the Core Case Service owns the case and the Tax Engine owns calculations.

column3: Define the DynamoDB queue projection table
column5: As a Backend Developer, I want a DynamoDB table for the Plan Cycle Queue projection, so that the queue is read from a denormalized store.
column6:
# A DynamoDB table holds a denormalized queue projection keyed by tenant_id with case sort key.
# Each item carries case ID, client, stage, owner, priority, due_date, and overdue flag.
# The table definition is created against a local DynamoDB for tests.

column3: Project Tax Plan Cycle changes into the queue table
column5: As a Backend Developer, I want cycle changes projected into the DynamoDB queue, so that the read model stays consistent with the case.
column6:
# Creating or updating a cycle upserts its queue projection item.
# The overdue flag is recomputed from due_date on each projection.
# A test asserts the projection matches the source cycle after a stage change.

column3: Cache the queue read in Redis with invalidation
column5: As an Advisor, I want the Plan Cycle Queue cached in Redis, so that the queue loads fast without hammering the read store.
column6:
# Queue reads check Redis first and fall back to DynamoDB on a miss.
# A cache entry is invalidated when a case's stage or due_date changes.
# A test asserts a stale entry is not served after an invalidating change.

column3: Store idempotency keys for case creation
column5: As a Backend Developer, I want an idempotency-key store, so that a retried create returns the original result.
column6:
# An idempotency record in Redis (idem:<key>, 24h TTL), keyed by the Idempotency-Key header, persists the first result.
# A repeat request with the same key returns the stored original result.
# Distinct keys create distinct cycles.

column3: Guard concurrent creates with the idempotency key
column5: As a Backend Developer, I want concurrent creates with the same key to produce one cycle, so that retries under load never duplicate cases.
column6:
# Two concurrent requests with the same Idempotency-Key create exactly one cycle.
# The second request is serialized by a Redis lock (lock:<key> via SET NX PX) and reads the first result rather than inserting again.
# A concurrency test asserts a single cycle is created.

column3: Document the storage decision matrix
